content.subtitle: Understanding Force and Motion
content.hookQuestion: Why does a heavier object require more force to move?
content.imagePrompt: A person pushing a light box vs a heavy box

bullets: Force is directly proportional to the product of mass and acceleration
a represents acceleration in meters per second squared (m/s²)
content.diagramPrompt: Vector diagram showing force, mass, and acceleration relationship with arrows

workedExample.question: A car of mass 1200 kg accelerates from rest to 20 m/s in 5 seconds. Calculate the net force acting on the car.
solutionSteps: First, calculate acceleration using: a = (v - u) / t
Now apply Newton's Second Law: F = ma
workedExample.finalAnswer: The net force acting on the car is 4800 N (or 4.8 kN)

content.diagramPrompt: Side view of a car with arrows showing initial position, final position, and force direction

workedExample.question: A force of 150 N causes an object to accelerate at 5 m/s². What is the mass of the object?
solutionSteps: Using Newton's Second Law: F = ma
Rearrange to solve for mass: m = F / a
Substitute the given values: m = 150 N / 5 m/s²
workedExample.finalAnswer: The mass of the object is 30 kg

content.notes: Remember to always check units: Force in Newtons, mass in kilograms, acceleration in m/s²

questionSet.stem: A 50 kg object accelerates at 2 m/s². What is the net force?
If force doubles while mass remains constant, acceleration will:
questionSet.explanation: Since F = ma, if F doubles and m is constant, a must also double

summaryPoints: Newton's Second Law: F = ma relates force, mass, and acceleration
Greater mass requires greater force for the same acceleration
The formula can be rearranged to find any unknown variable

activity.prompt: A 10 kg box is pushed with a force of 40 N. Calculate the acceleration of the box. Show your work!
